 Ticketmaster Names New CTO Amid Brazil Data Breach

 Ticketmaster is expanding its technology leadership while facing questions about a customer data breach in Brazil that exposed personal information and ticket-purchase records. The Live Nation-owned ticketing company appointed former Amazon Prime Video vice president Jim Freeman as chief technology officer, announcing the leadership change on October 20, 2026, as the scope and timing of the Brazilian security incident remained unclear.
 According to Music Industry Weekly, Freeman will lead an "AI-first" strategy across Ticketmaster's technology operations. The company also appointed Rachel Smith, who joins from Block, and Chuck Mortimore, a former Disney executive, as senior vice presidents, strengthening its leadership team as it pursues technology and engineering improvements.
 Advertisement 
 Scroll To Continue with Content 
 Separately, Ticketmaster confirmed a data breach affecting Brazilian customers who purchased tickets during 2025. According to TicketNews, the exposed information potentially included names, contact details, residential location information, dates of birth or age ranges, government identification records, and ticket-purchase details.

 The affected records may also have included Brazil's CPF taxpayer identification numbers, payment methods, and the final four digits of credit cards. The information involved varied according to the details customers supplied when buying tickets. Ticketmaster has not disclosed the number of affected customers or identified the third-party analytics provider involved.
 Ticketmaster attributed the incident to a temporary vulnerability in an external data analytics tool rather than its primary ticketing infrastructure. The company said it took immediate steps to contain the incident and launched an investigation with outside cybersecurity specialists.
 "The ticket sales platform and fan account systems were not affected," Ticketmaster said in a statement provided to Brazilian media, according to TicketNews.
 Also Read 
 TFG London Warns Customers After Cybersecurity Incident 
 The company also maintained that account passwords, complete credit card numbers, and bank account numbers were not compromised. It has not established publicly whether the incident affected individuals outside Brazil or disclosed the precise date the vulnerability was exploited.
 Ticketmaster began notifying affected customers on October 14, according to TicketNews. Brazilian technology publication Canaltech reported that the company's investigation, conducted with external cybersecurity specialists, had concluded in September 2026. However, the exact date the incident was discovered and when the company determined that personal information had been exposed remain undisclosed.
 Those dates are relevant to Brazil's data protection requirements. Under Resolution CD/ANPD No. 15/2024, organizations generally must notify the national data protection regulator, known as the ANPD, and affected individuals within three business days of becoming aware of a qualifying incident involving personal data and potential risk or significant harm.
 Also Read 
 FBI Arrests Cybersecurity Firm Co-Founder in ShinyHunters Probe 
 The reported gap between the investigation's conclusion and customer notifications does not, by itself, establish a regulatory violation. Determining compliance requires additional information about when Ticketmaster became aware that personal data had been affected and when the required notifications were made.
 Brazilian technology publication Olhar Digital reported on October 15 that Ticketmaster had confirmed notifying the ANPD, although the company did not disclose the date of that notification. The regulator acknowledged a request for information from TicketNews and said the inquiry had been referred to its technical department.
 "We received your inquiry and forwarded it to the technical department," the ANPD's communications office said in an email response translated from Portuguese, according to TicketNews.
 Also Read 
 ASOS App Sends Hacked Push Notifications To Users 
 The regulator's acknowledgment does not confirm that it has opened a formal investigation or identified compliance concerns. TicketNews also sought information from Ticketmaster and Live Nation about the number of affected customers, the third-party provider, possible international exposure, and any connection to other cybersecurity incidents. Neither company had provided substantive answers to those questions at publication.
 The Brazilian disclosure follows a separate incident reported by Live Nation to the Vermont Attorney General's Office on October 1. That disclosure involved Social Security numbers, government identification records, and health information. Three proposed class action lawsuits were filed against Live Nation in federal court in California on October 6 and 7, alleging inadequate protection of sensitive personal information.
 Live Nation described the US incident as limited in scope, involving a small number of individuals without disrupting operations. Two plaintiffs identified themselves as former employees, raising questions about whether the compromised information primarily involved employment records. The company has not publicly established a connection between that incident and the Brazilian Ticketmaster breach.
 Also Read 
 CenterPoint Energy Data Breach Exposes Customer Information in September 
 The Brazilian incident also follows Ticketmaster's 2024 data breach involving customer information stored in a third-party Snowflake cloud database. Live Nation previously confirmed unauthorized access to Ticketmaster information in that database, although it did not independently verify all claims made by hackers about the number of records stolen.
